title: 160 Meter Band
snippet: Primarily a night-time band; heavy static in summer thunderstorm season. Voice activity mostly above 1.840–1.900 MHz.

title: 80/75 Meter Band
snippet: Good regional night-time HF band; popular for regional nets and ragchews.

title: 60 Meter Band (Channelized)
snippet: 4 channel centers: 5332.0, 5348.0, 5373.0, 5405.0 kHz, plus a reduced-power secondary WRC-15 segment at 5351.5–5366.5 kHz. Rules here changed as recently as December 2025 - reverify current rules before any transmit use.
freq: 5330.5–5406.4 kHz (4 fixed channels + a lower-power secondary segment)

title: 40 Meter Band
snippet: Reliable regional/continental night-time HF band; one of the most consistently active ham HF bands after dark.

title: 30 Meter Band
snippet: Narrow shared band; mostly CW and FT8/other digital activity, rarely voice.

title: 20 Meter Band
snippet: The most popular HF DX (long-distance) band; often active worldwide nearly any time of day.

title: 17 Meter Band
snippet: WARC band (no contests permitted); good daytime DX band.

title: 15 Meter Band
snippet: Daytime band, strongly tied to the solar/sunspot cycle - can be excellent or nearly dead depending on solar activity.

title: 12 Meter Band
snippet: WARC band; narrow, daytime, solar-cycle dependent.

title: 10 Meter Band
snippet: FM repeaters/simplex cluster near 29.520–29.680 MHz. Otherwise very solar-cycle dependent - can be nearly dead for years, then open worldwide during high solar activity.

title: 6 Meter Band
snippet: Nicknamed ‘the Magic Band’ - usually quiet, but sporadic-E and other propagation can unpredictably open it for long-distance contacts.

title: 2 Meter Band
snippet: The most popular VHF ham band. National FM simplex calling frequency: 146.520 MHz. FM repeater outputs are commonly found across 144–148 MHz per local band plan.

title: 1.25 Meter Band
snippet: Less common band - fewer radios support it. 222.100 MHz is a widely-used national simplex calling frequency in many regions.

title: 70 Centimeter Band
snippet: Second most popular ham VHF/UHF band after 2m. National FM simplex calling frequency: 446.000 MHz. Widely used for repeaters and digital voice (DMR/D-STAR/System Fusion).

title: AM Broadcast (Mediumwave)
snippet: AM travels far at night via skywave (ionospheric) propagation - distant stations often become audible after dark that are inaudible during the day.
freq: 535–1705 kHz (540–1700 kHz channelized, 10 kHz spacing, 117 channels)

title: FM Broadcast
snippet: Line-of-sight VHF propagation - range is mostly limited by antenna height/terrain, not time of day (unlike AM).

title: Shortwave Broadcast
snippet: Best reception varies a lot by band, time of day, and season - lower bands tend to favor night reception, higher bands favor daytime; all of it is sensitive to solar activity.

title: NOAA Weather Radio (All Hazards)
snippet: Continuous weather broadcast plus All Hazards alerts (severe weather and some non-weather emergencies). Typical range ~40 miles from a full-power transmitter over level terrain. Coverage depends on the specific transmitter serving your location, not just your state. Channel numbering (WX1–WX7) is a common radio-manufacturer convention, not an official NOAA designation - confirm by frequency, not channel number.

title: Citizens Band (CB) Radio
snippet: Normally short-range ground-wave propagation (a few miles), but can skip long distances during sporadic-E or other solar/atmospheric conditions.

title: FRS (Family Radio Service)
snippet: Real-world range is usually well under 1 mile in typical terrain, despite marketing claims of much longer range.

title: GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service)
snippet: Repeaters can extend usable range to roughly 20+ miles depending on antenna height/terrain. Per a 2024 FCC clarification, GMRS repeaters may not be linked to each other over the internet.
freq: 462.550–467.725 MHz (22 shared channels + repeater input pairs on ch.15-22)

title: MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service)
snippet: Generally less crowded than FRS/GMRS in many areas; popular for trail, farm, and property use.

title: Marine VHF
snippet: Channel 16 = international distress/calling/safety. Channel 9 = recreational hailing (alternate to 16 in many areas). Channel 13 = bridge-to-bridge navigation safety. Channel 22A/1022 = USCG safety/weather announcements. Channel 70 = digital calling only, no voice.

title: Aviation / Airband
snippet: Deliberately uses AM, not FM - lets a stronger nearby signal be heard over a weaker one instead of one completely blocking the other ('capture effect'), which matters for safety. Standard US channel spacing is 25 kHz (8.33 kHz in parts of Europe). HF (2.850–22 MHz, USB) is used for oceanic/remote-area voice beyond VHF range.

title: Railroad Radio
snippet: Uses an AAR-coordinated channel plan (roughly 97 channels, 15 kHz spacing) for dispatch, road/yard operations, and defect detectors. Specific channel-to-railroad/purpose assignments are regional and change over time - consult a current regional scanner/railfan frequency guide for your area rather than relying on a fixed list here.
freq: approximately 159.6–161.6 MHz (exact lower edge unconfirmed - see note)

title: AM (Amplitude Modulation)
snippet: Signal strength (amplitude) varies to carry sound. Simple and tolerant of weak-signal fading, and lets a stronger station be heard over a weaker one on the same frequency instead of blocking it outright.

title: FM / NFM (Narrowband Frequency Modulation)
snippet: Signal frequency varies slightly to carry sound. Used for most two-way land-mobile voice. Generally clearer than AM in strong-signal conditions, but the weaker of two same-frequency signals is usually blocked entirely (the 'capture effect') rather than heard faintly underneath.

title: WFM (Wideband FM)
snippet: Wide-deviation FM used for commercial FM broadcast - much higher audio fidelity than narrowband FM, but uses far more bandwidth. On a wideband receiver, WFM is usually a separate mode setting from (N)FM, not the same one.

title: USB (Upper Sideband)
snippet: A form of single-sideband voice (roughly half of an AM signal, more efficient for a given power). Used by amateur-radio convention above 10 MHz, plus HF airband and marine SSB. Sounds badly garbled if tuned even slightly off-frequency - fine adjustment matters.

title: LSB (Lower Sideband)
snippet: The other half of single-sideband voice - same technical concept as USB, just the other sideband. Used by amateur-radio convention on 160m/80m/60m/40m. The USB/LSB split by band is a long-standing operating custom, not a technical requirement.

title: CW (Continuous Wave / Morse Code)
snippet: The carrier is simply switched on and off to send Morse code - no voice. Extremely narrow bandwidth, so CW signals can often be copied through noise/interference where a voice signal couldn't.

title: RF Spectrum Overview
snippet: The usable radio spectrum for a wideband receiver like a Malahit spans roughly 100 kHz to 2+ GHz depending on the model. Moving up in frequency: LF/MF holds AM

snippet: HF (High Frequency, 3–30 MHz) can travel worldwide by bouncing off the ionosphere ('skywave'), especially at night - this is how shortwave broadcast and long-di

snippet: HF signals can travel very long distances by refracting off the ionosphere back down to earth ('skywave'), but how well this works depends heavily on time of da

title: What to Monitor During Severe Weather / an Emergency
snippet: Start with NOAA Weather Radio (162.400–162.550 MHz, NFM) for official forecasts and All Hazards alerts - it's the single most reliable receive-only source here.

title: Decibels (dB / dBm) - Signal Strength Concepts
snippet: A decibel (dB) is a ratio, not an absolute amount - it compares two power levels on a logarithmic scale. +3 dB means roughly double the power; +10 dB means 10x

title: Software-Defined Radio (SDR) Basics
snippet: A traditional radio does its filtering/demodulation in dedicated analog hardware built for one job. An SDR instead digitizes a chunk of raw spectrum as early as

snippet: Simplex means two stations talk directly to each other on one shared frequency - simple, but range is limited to whatever the two stations can reach directly (l

title: Antenna Polarization
snippet: Polarization describes the orientation of a radio wave's electric field, and it's set by the physical orientation of the transmitting antenna - vertical (antenn

snippet: The cable between a radio and its antenna (the 'feed line', almost always coax at these frequencies) loses some signal as heat over its length - loss increases

title: SWR & Impedance Matching
snippet: Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) measures how well an antenna's impedance matches the feed line and transmitter feeding it - a perfect match is 1:1; anything higher me

title: Microwave & Waveguide Basics
snippet: At high enough frequencies (roughly above 1 GHz, well into the microwave range used by radar, satellite links, and Wi-Fi), ordinary coaxial cable becomes increa

title: NATO Phonetic Alphabet
snippet: The standard spelling alphabet used internationally on radio and telephone to make letters unambiguous over a noisy channel (e.g. 'B' and 'D' sound alike, but '

title: Morse Code Reference
snippet: International Morse Code - a series of short ('dit') and long ('dah', roughly 3x a dit's length) tones representing letters and digits. Still used today on amat

title: Watch vs. Warning vs. Advisory: What NWS Alert Terms Mean
snippet: These three words carry specific, different meanings on NOAA Weather Radio and every other official alert channel - mixing them up changes what action is actual

title: CW (Morse Code)
snippet: A single steady tone switching on and off in short (dit) and long (dah) bursts - unmistakable once heard. Often sounds musical/rhythmic from a skilled operator.

title: SSB Voice (Single Sideband)
snippet: If tuned slightly off-frequency, voice sounds high-pitched, garbled, or 'Donald Duck'-like - this is the single most reliable SSB identifier. Correctly tuned, i

title: AM Voice / Broadcast
snippet: Full, natural-sounding voice/music with no 'quieting' effect - background static fades in/out smoothly rather than snapping open/closed like FM squelch. On airb

title: NFM Voice (Narrowband FM)
snippet: Clean, quiet audio when a signal is present; squelch snaps fully open/closed rather than fading gradually the way AM/SSB static does. Weak signals often 'pop' o

title: NOAA SAME / EAS Digital Alert Burst
snippet: A distinctive harsh, buzzing warble lasting a few seconds, immediately before a spoken weather alert - this is the Specific Area Message Encoding (SAME) header

title: DTMF (Touch-Tone)
snippet: The familiar telephone keypad tones - a short burst of one or more distinct two-tone beeps. On amateur/business radio, usually heard briefly at the start of a t

title: RTTY (Radioteletype)
snippet: A steady two-tone warbling/trilling sound at a constant rhythm - distinctly more mechanical and continuous than CW's dit-dah pattern. Sounds a little like an ol

title: Packet / APRS Burst
snippet: A brief (roughly 1 second), harsh, buzzing burst - often described as sounding like a short 'brrrt' or a modem handshake fragment. Position/status data (APRS) o

title: Thunderstorms & Lightning
snippet: If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck.

title: Beaufort Wind Scale (Estimating Wind Speed by Eye)
snippet: Estimate wind speed just by watching smoke, leaves, trees, and flags - no instruments needed.

title: Tornadoes
snippet: Get to the lowest, most interior, windowless room you can, right away.

title: Flooding
snippet: Turn Around, Don't Drown - never walk, swim, or drive through flood water.

title: Earthquakes
snippet: Drop, Cover, and Hold On the moment you feel shaking.

title: Wildfire & Smoke
snippet: Evacuate immediately if told to; otherwise reduce smoke exposure indoors.

title: Extreme Heat
snippet: Recognize heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke - heat stroke is a 911 emergency.

title: Extreme Cold & Winter Weather
snippet: Hypothermia and frostbite both need warmth first - know the signs.

title: When the Power Goes Out
snippet: Keep freezers/fridges closed and have a plan for medical devices.

title: Downed Power Lines
snippet: Assume every downed line is live - stay back and call it in.

title: Generator Safety
snippet: Generators belong outside, far from windows - never in a garage or basement.

title: Carbon Monoxide Safety
snippet: CO is invisible and odorless - symptoms feel like the flu.

title: Alternative Lighting & Fire Safety
snippet: Use flashlights instead of candles during an outage.

title: Water Storage & Boil-Water Advisories
snippet: Store 1 gallon per person per day; follow local guidance on advisories.

title: Food Safety During an Outage
snippet: When in doubt, throw it out.

title: Sanitation Without Running Water
snippet: Plan for toilets before you need one - poor sanitation spreads disease fast.

title: Family Emergency Communication Plan
snippet: Pick an out-of-town contact - long-distance calls/texts often work when local ones don't.

title: Evacuation
snippet: If told to evacuate, go - don't wait to see how bad it gets.

title: Shelter-in-Place vs. Evacuating
snippet: Sometimes staying put is safer than trying to leave.

title: When Phones & Internet Are Down
snippet: Text over talk, and know your offline fallback.

title: Battery & Power Conservation
snippet: Assume you won't be able to recharge - make it last.

title: Pets in an Emergency
snippet: If it's not safe for you to stay, it's not safe for your pet either.

title: Ground-to-Air Emergency Signals
snippet: Six standardized symbols any search-and-rescue aircrew worldwide is trained to recognize - useful when radio and phones are both out.

title: International Emergency Numbers
snippet: 911 is a North American convention, not a global one - know the local number before you need it.

title: Ten Essentials for Outdoor/Field Safety
snippet: A standard packing checklist that covers navigation, sun/weather protection, food/water, and emergency shelter for any outdoor trip.

title: Chemical Water Disinfection (Bleach, Iodine, Tablets)
snippet: When boiling isn't possible, unscented household bleach, iodine, or chlorine dioxide tablets can disinfect small quantities of water - with real limits.

title: Get Professional Help - Check, Call, Care
snippet: Scene safety first, then call 911 for anything life-threatening.

title: CPR / AED Overview
snippet: For an unresponsive person not breathing normally: call 911, get an AED, and begin CPR if trained.

title: Choking (Conscious Adult/Child)
snippet: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears.

title: Severe (Life-Threatening) Bleeding
snippet: Direct pressure first; a tourniquet if bleeding on a limb won't stop.

title: Shock
snippet: Pale, cool, clammy skin and a fast weak pulse are early warning signs.

title: Burns
snippet: Cool the burn under clean, cool running water for 10-20 minutes.

title: Minor Cuts & Wounds
snippet: Clean it, cover it, and watch for signs of infection.

title: Sprains & Fractures
snippet: Rest, immobilize, cool, and elevate - don't try to straighten a deformed limb.

title: Head Injury Warning Signs
snippet: Watch closely after any bump to the head - some warning signs appear later.

title: Seizures
snippet: Protect them from injury - don't restrain, and don't put anything in their mouth.

title: Poisoning
snippet: Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or 911 - don't guess at home remedies.

title: Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis
snippet: Anaphylaxis can turn life-threatening within minutes - epinephrine, not antihistamines, is the treatment.

title: Heat Exhaustion & Heat Stroke
snippet: Heat stroke (hot, dry/red skin, confusion) is a 911 emergency - cool the person immediately.

title: Hypothermia & Frostbite
snippet: Warm the person gradually - never with direct high heat, and never rub frostbitten skin.

title: Insect Bites, Stings & Snake Bites
snippet: Watch for allergic reaction after any sting; call 911 immediately for any snake bite.

title: First-Aid Kit Reference
snippet: A basic kit covers most minor injuries and buys time for anything bigger.

title: Bowline
snippet: A fixed loop at the end of a line that won't slip or jam - the classic "rescue loop," but not a life-safety knot on its own.

title: Figure-Eight Stopper Knot
snippet: A thick, easy-to-untie knot tied in the end of a rope so it can't pull through a pulley, block, or grommet.

title: Square Knot (Reef Knot)
snippet: Joins two ropes of similar thickness for light, non-critical purposes - notoriously unsafe for anything that actually needs to hold.

title: Sheet Bend
snippet: Joins two ropes - especially two of different thickness, or wet/slippery cordage - more securely than a square knot.

title: Clove Hitch
snippet: A quick hitch around a post or pole - fast to tie and untie, but can slip if the pull direction shifts around.

title: Two Half Hitches (Round Turn and Two Half Hitches)
snippet: A dependable way to tie a line to a post, ring, or tree - more secure than a clove hitch alone.

title: Taut-Line Hitch
snippet: An adjustable friction hitch that holds under tension but slides to re-tension by hand - ideal for tent and tarp guy lines.

title: Trucker's Hitch (Overview)
snippet: A mechanical-advantage hitch for cinching a load down tight - genuinely useful, but the hardest knot on this list to learn from text alone.

title: Levers & Mechanical Advantage
snippet: Every lever trades force for distance, or distance for force - never both at once.

title: Pulleys & Block and Tackle
snippet: More rope through more pulleys means less force needed - but more rope to pull.

title: Fastener Basics: Screws, Bolts & Nuts
snippet: "Screw" and "bolt" aren't interchangeable - the difference is how the fastener is meant to be tightened.

title: Torque Concepts
snippet: Torque is a twisting force applied at a distance - and "tight enough" has a real upper limit, not just a lower one.

title: Bearings & Lubrication
snippet: A bearing's whole job is turning sliding friction into much lower rolling friction - and it fails when that stops happening.

title: Common Hand Tools: Choosing the Right One
snippet: Most hand-tool damage and injuries come from using the almost-right tool instead of stopping to find the right one.

title: Mechanical Measurement: Calipers & Micrometers
snippet: A steel rule measures to about 1/64 inch by eye; calipers and micrometers measure far more precisely than that.

title: A Practical Approach to Mechanical Troubleshooting
snippet: Find out what actually changed before you start taking things apart.

title: Voltage, Current, Resistance & Power
snippet: Four quantities, one relationship (Ohm's Law) - understand these and most basic circuit behavior follows.

title: AC Fundamentals
snippet: Unlike DC, alternating current reverses direction on a regular cycle - which is exactly why AC voltage/current values need their own way of being expressed.

title: Semiconductors: Diodes & Transistors
snippet: A diode lets current flow one way only; a transistor uses a small current/voltage to control a much larger one.

title: Circuit Protection: Fuses & Breakers
snippet: Both fuses and breakers exist to fail on purpose, safely, before a wire or component fails unsafely.

title: Switches & Relays
snippet: A relay is just a switch that's controlled electrically instead of by hand.

title: Analog vs. Digital Fundamentals
snippet: Analog represents a value as a continuously variable quantity; digital represents it as discrete on/off states.

title: GHS Hazard Pictograms
snippet: The nine standardized symbols used on chemical labels to show what kind of hazard a substance presents - the fastest way to size up a container before reading anything else on it.

title: Reading a Safety Data Sheet (SDS)
snippet: Every hazardous chemical sold commercially is required to have a Safety Data Sheet - a standardized, 16-section document that says far more than the label ever could. Knowing the section layout means finding the one fact needed without reading the whole thing.

title: Exposure Limits and PPE Selection Logic
snippet: Occupational exposure limits (like an OSHA PEL or NIOSH REL) describe how much of a substance in air is considered acceptable over a work shift - understanding the shape of that number matters more than memorizing any single value.

title: Recognizing Categories of Chemical Hazard
snippet: Beyond the pictograms themselves, chemical hazards fall into a few broad families worth recognizing on sight: physical hazards (fire/reactivity), health hazards (toxicity), and environmental hazards - each calling for a different kind of caution.

title: Basic Material Properties for Repair and Handling
snippet: A handful of everyday material properties explain most of why one material is chosen over another for a repair or a container - hardness, strength, corrosion resistance, and flammability chief among them.

title: General Safe Storage and Handling Principles
snippet: A short set of general-purpose habits - not tied to any one chemical - that reduce risk across almost any hazardous-materials situation: labeling, segregation, ventilation, and never relying on memory.

title: Chemical Storage Groups: Keeping Incompatibles Apart
snippet: A lettered scheme (compatible organic/inorganic acids, bases, oxidizers, pyrophorics, and more) for grouping chemicals so incompatible ones never share a shelf, plus what to look for when inspecting a storage area.

title: Subnet
snippet: A smaller network carved out of a larger one, sharing a defined range of addresses.

title: CIDR
snippet: A compact way to write how big a network is, as a slash-number after an IP address (e.g. /24).

title: DHCP
snippet: The service that automatically hands a joining device its IP address, subnet, gateway, and DNS server.

title: DNS
snippet: The lookup service that translates a domain name (example.com) into an IP address.

title: Checksum / Hash
snippet: A short fixed-length fingerprint calculated from a file's contents, used to verify it wasn't corrupted or altered.

title: Character Encoding
snippet: The rule a computer uses to turn stored bytes back into readable text.

title: Serial (RS-232/UART)
snippet: A simple one-bit-at-a-time connection standard, still common for consoles on embedded/networking gear.

title: Polarization
snippet: The orientation of a radio wave's electric field - vertical, horizontal, or circular - set by the transmitting antenna.

title: Impedance
snippet: A circuit or cable's opposition to AC current flow - RF gear is almost always designed around 50 ohms.

title: SWR (Standing Wave Ratio)
snippet: A measure of how well an antenna system's impedance is matched - 1:1 is a perfect match, higher numbers mean more reflected signal.

title: Modulation
snippet: How information (voice, data) is impressed onto a radio wave for transmission.

title: Simplex
snippet: Direct radio-to-radio communication on one frequency, with no repeater in between.

title: Repeater
snippet: A fixed station, usually on a hill/tower, that receives a signal and instantly retransmits it to extend range.

title: dB / dBm
snippet: Logarithmic units for comparing signal strength - dB is a ratio, dBm is an absolute power level referenced to 1 milliwatt.

title: Declination
snippet: The angle between true (map) north and magnetic (compass) north at a given location.

title: Datum
snippet: The specific mathematical model of the Earth's shape a coordinate is measured against - the same coordinates can shift if the datum differs.

title: Contour Interval
snippet: The elevation difference represented between one contour line and the next on a topographic map.

title: Bearing
snippet: The clockwise angle from north to whatever direction you're pointing or heading.

title: Latitude / Longitude
snippet: The universal coordinate pair for any point on Earth - how far north/south (latitude) and east/west (longitude) of two reference lines.

title: UTM
snippet: Universal Transverse Mercator - divides the world into 60 numbered zones, giving position as a meters-based easting/northing.

title: MGRS
snippet: Military Grid Reference System - the same UTM grid, but identifies the 100km square with letters instead of numbers.

title: Voltage
snippet: Electrical potential difference - the "pressure" that pushes current through a circuit, measured in volts.

title: Current
snippet: The actual flow of electric charge through a circuit, measured in amps.

title: Resistance
snippet: How much a component opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms.

title: Power (Electrical)
snippet: The rate of energy use or transfer in a circuit, measured in watts.

title: SI Prefix
snippet: A standard multiplier (kilo, milli, mega, etc.) that means the same thing regardless of which unit it's attached to.

title: Beaufort Scale
snippet: An international 0-12 scale for estimating wind speed just by observing its effects - no instruments needed.

title: Watch vs. Warning
snippet: A watch means conditions are favorable for a hazard; a warning means it's happening or imminent - act now.

title: IPv4 Addressing Basics
snippet: An IPv4 address is four numbers (0-255) separated by dots - every device on a network needs one to be reached.

title: Private IP Address Ranges & Loopback
snippet: Certain address ranges are reserved for private networks and never routed on the public internet.

title: CIDR Prefix <-> Subnet Mask Reference
snippet: A /24 and a 255.255.255.0 subnet mask are two ways of writing the exact same thing.

title: DNS & DHCP: What They Actually Do
snippet: DNS translates names to addresses; DHCP hands out addresses automatically - two different jobs, often confused.

title: Common Ports & Protocols
snippet: A port number identifies which specific service on a device a connection is meant for.

title: Wi-Fi Terminology
snippet: SSID, band, and security-standard terms explained plainly.

title: Ethernet & Cabling Basics
snippet: RJ45 connectors, cable categories, and why 'crossover cable' advice is mostly obsolete now.

title: USB & Serial Basics
snippet: USB-C is a connector shape, not a speed - and serial devices need both ends to agree on a baud rate.

title: Checksums & Hashes: Verifying File Integrity
snippet: A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of a file's contents - useful for catching corruption or tampering.

title: Text Encoding: ASCII, UTF-8 & Unicode
snippet: Garbled text on screen is usually a wrong encoding guess, not corrupted data.

title: Latitude & Longitude Basics
snippet: Latitude = how far north/south of the equator; longitude = how far east/west of the Prime Meridian.

title: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)
snippet: The same location can be written several different ways - know which one your device/map uses.

title: How GPS Works Without Internet
snippet: GPS gets your position from satellites directly - it never needed the internet or cell service.

title: Cardinal Directions & Compass Bearings
snippet: N/E/S/W at 90° intervals; a bearing is the clockwise angle from north to your target.

title: Basic Offline Navigation Concepts
snippet: A paper map, a compass, and knowing your last confirmed position go a long way with zero electronics.

title: Map Scale
snippet: A representative fraction like 1:24,000 means 1 unit on the map equals 24,000 of the same unit on the ground.

title: Reading Contour Lines
snippet: Each contour line connects points of equal elevation - spacing and shape tell you the terrain's steepness and form.

title: True North vs. Magnetic North
snippet: A map's grid points to true (geographic) north; a compass needle points to magnetic north - the angle between them is declination.

title: United States Time Zones
snippet: 9 official US time zones exist under the Uniform Time Act - not all of them observe daylight saving time.

title: World Time Zones: UTC Reference Points
snippet: A selection of reference points across the UTC range - not a complete list of every zone.

title: World Reference Map
snippet: Static offline world map - country borders, equirectangular projection.

title: United States Reference Map
snippet: Static offline US map - state borders, CONUS + Alaska/Hawaii insets.

title: Local Information
snippet: Emergency management, NWS office, hospitals, shelters, amateur repeaters, and other resources for this PirateBox's current location.

title: Emergency (police/fire/medical)
snippet: 911 - Universal in the US - not region-specific.

title: Poison Control
snippet: 1-800-222-1222 - National Poison Control Center - free, 24/7, works from anywhere in the US. Same number cited in the First Aid section.

title: Map Reading and Land Navigation (FM 3-25.26 / FM 21-26)
snippet: The US Army's full field manual on map reading and land navigation - topographic map symbols and marginal information, grid systems (UTM/MGRS in full detail), compass use, declination, terrain association, and both day and night navigation techniques. Directly complements this device's own coordinate-format and true-vs-magnetic-north reference with the complete authoritative procedure behind it.

title: United States Frequency Allocation Chart
snippet: The official wall chart showing which service (broadcast, amateur, aviation, marine, federal, etc.) is allocated to every band from 3 kHz to 300 GHz - the authoritative big-picture answer to "what's using this part of the spectrum," complementing this device's own per-service Radio Reference and signal-identification framework.

title: Electrical Safety (OSHA QuickCard)
snippet: A concise official safety card on basic electrical hazards - shock, arc flash/blast, and safe work practices around electrical equipment. Pairs with this device's own Ohm's Law/AWG reference and multimeter-safety note with an authoritative original on the hazards themselves.

title: Controlling Electrical Hazards (OSHA 3075)
snippet: The full-length OSHA booklet behind the QuickCard above: how electricity flows, what causes shocks and burns, what to do if someone "freezes" to a live contact, insulation/guarding/grounding, GFCIs, static electricity, lockout/tagout, and safe work practices - real depth beyond a one-page summary.

title: Preparing for Emergencies: Guide for Communities
snippet: The UK Cabinet Office's household/community emergency-preparedness guide - risk awareness, a household emergency plan, and a basic emergency kit list. A genuinely international counterpart to this library's otherwise US-federal-sourced emergency guidance, useful anywhere this device might travel, not just in the US.

title: Topographic Map Symbols
snippet: The official USGS legend for topographic map symbols - contours, boundaries, vegetation, hydrography, transportation, and structures - the standard reference for reading a USGS topo map.

title: NIST Time and Frequency Services (NIST Special Publication 432)
snippet: NIST's comprehensive reference on time and frequency measurement, calibration, and broadcast services (WWV/WWVB, GPS timing, NTP) - the authoritative technical background behind the time-confidence concepts this device's own Field Tools/status pages already surface.

title: Sky Watcher Cloud Chart
snippet: A visual cloud-identification chart (cirrus, cumulus, stratus, and their combinations/altitudes) for identifying cloud types by sight - useful alongside this device's severe-weather monitoring guidance.

title: Thunderstorms, Tornadoes, Lightning... A Preparedness Guide
snippet: NOAA National Weather Service preparedness guide covering thunderstorms, tornadoes, lightning, straight-line winds, flash floods, and hail - what makes each hazard dangerous, watch-vs-warning terminology, and specific life-saving actions for each, including a dedicated section on tornado safety in schools.

title: Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)
snippet: NIST's authoritative guide to the SI (metric) system: base and derived units, prefixes, and a comprehensive Appendix B conversion-factors table between US customary/imperial units and SI units, plus rules for correct unit usage and rounding. Fills a general-purpose measurement/conversion reference gap - useful well beyond any single subject page.

title: Make Water Safe During an Emergency
snippet: CDC fact sheet on making water safe to drink after an emergency or disaster - boiling, chemical disinfection, and filtering, with the important limitation that fuel/chemical/radioactive contamination cannot be fixed by any of these methods.

title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
snippet: EPA two-page fact sheet with specific bleach-dosing measurements (drops per quart/liter/gallon at two different bleach concentrations), a granular calcium hypochlorite (HTH) method, and an iodine tincture method for disinfecting water when boiling isn't possible - concrete dosing detail that complements rather than duplicates the existing CDC water-safety fact sheet, which covers methods at a higher level without exact measurements.

title: Family Emergency Communication Plan
snippet: FEMA/Ready.gov's full fillable family emergency communication plan - household contact info, out-of-town contact, meeting places, school/work emergency plans, and important medical/insurance information in one printable document.

title: Food and Water Safety During Power Outages and Floods
snippet: FDA consumer factsheet on keeping food and water safe during a power outage or flood - refrigerator/freezer safe-time thresholds, a food-safety decision guide (when to keep vs. discard), and water safety/treatment basics. A different USDA FSIS candidate on this same general topic was blocked by durable HTTP 403 bot protection; this FDA document independently covers the same subject and was confirmed directly accessible and public domain.

title: First Aid (FM 4-25.11 / NTRP 4-02.1 / AFMAN 44-163(I))
snippet: The joint US military field manual on first aid - full step-by-step procedures with illustrations for airway/breathing/bleeding control, shock, fractures/splinting, burns, cold/heat injury, bites/stings, and evacuation/transport techniques. Addresses the visual-diagram gap the First Aid Reference page's own audit flagged (pressure points, tourniquets, fracture types, splinting, etc.) with an authoritative, fully redistributable original source, after Red Cross material was found not to be freely redistributable. Note: this manual does not include recovery-position content - checked directly via full-text search, not assumed.

title: Rigging Techniques, Procedures, and Applications (FM 5-125)
snippet: US Army field manual on rope, wire rope, and chain rigging: fiber/wire rope characteristics and care, knots/hitches/bends/splices/lashings, slings, blocks and tackle, chain hoists and winches, and rope ladders. Source for a small, verified set of correctly-depicted knot diagrams added to the Outdoor/Field knots reference, which previously had text-only entries specifically because no verified-correct diagram source had been confirmed.

title: Reduce Your Smoke Exposure (Wildfire Smoke Factsheet)
snippet: EPA factsheet on reducing exposure to wildfire smoke - indoor/outdoor precautions, air cleaners, and who is at greater risk, developed through interagency collaboration including the US Forest Service.

title: How to Prepare and Store Powdered Infant Formula During an Emergency
snippet: Current CDC step-by-step guidance for safely preparing powdered infant formula when tap water is unsafe (natural disaster, drinking-water outage): using bottled/boiled/disinfected water, exact measurement, storage/discard timing, and a clear warning to prefer ready-to-feed formula for infants under 2 months, premature, or immunocompromised. Fills a genuine gap - infant/child feeding safety - not covered by any other retained document.

title: Community Recovery (Australian Disaster Resilience Handbook 2)
snippet: Australian Institute for Disaster Resilience handbook on what happens after a disaster: social/psychological recovery, financial and built-environment recovery, and how communities organize recovery efforts. Complements this library's existing before/during-disaster material (all US and UK sources) with substantive after-the-fact guidance, and is this library's second clearly-licensed non-US source.

title: Fastener Design Manual (NASA RP-1228)
snippet: NASA's authoritative reference on threaded fasteners: material selection, platings/lubricants, corrosion, locking methods, washers/inserts, thread types and classes, torque formulas, fatigue loading, grip length, head styles, and fastener strength, plus rivets and lockbolts. Establishes the new Mechanical & Basic Repair area of the library with a genuinely deep, non-hazardous reference (understanding fasteners, not performing certified repairs).

title: Plane Geometry (Wentworth, 1899)
snippet: A classic, complete plane geometry textbook - lines, angles, triangles, circles, polygons, area/proportion, and geometric construction with straightedge and compass - proofs and constructions whose validity hasn't changed since publication. Retained as a historical public-domain work for a durable, non-safety-critical subject (geometry), clearly dated rather than presented as current.

title: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NEETS Module 10)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on RF fundamentals: how radio waves propagate, transmission line theory and characteristic impedance, standing waves/SWR, impedance matching, and antenna types and behavior. Fills the Radio/RF depth gap beyond the frequency-allocation chart with real technical fundamentals, without touching any copyrighted ARRL material.

title: Introduction to Number Systems and Logic (NEETS Module 13)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on binary/octal/hexadecimal number systems, conversions between them, binary arithmetic and binary-coded decimal, Boolean algebra, and logic gates/circuits - the foundational digital-computing concepts behind all modern networking and computing equipment. Establishes the new Computing & Digital Fundamentals area of the library.

title: Basic Machines (NAVEDTRA 14037)
snippet: Navy self-study training course on the six simple machines (lever, wheel and axle, block and tackle, gears, wedge, inclined plane/screw) and their combinations in real mechanical devices - mechanical advantage, gear ratios, and friction/bearings/lubrication. Directly complements the Fastener Design Manual with the mechanical-principle side of Mechanical & Basic Repair.

title: American Practical Navigator (Bowditch)
snippet: The classic, encyclopedic reference on navigation without electronics: piloting, dead reckoning, tides and currents, and full celestial navigation (sextant use, sight reduction, the nautical almanac, time and celestial coordinate systems). Genuinely one of the most valuable offline references imaginable for a device meant to help when GPS/electronics aren't available - teaches navigation methods that work with nothing but a sextant, a chronometer, and this book.

title: Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current (NEETS Module 1)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on DC electrical fundamentals: atomic theory of electricity, conductors/insulators/semiconductors, static electricity, magnetism, and DC circuit theory (Ohm's law, series/parallel circuits, Kirchhoff's laws). The foundational module beneath the wave-propagation/antenna and test-equipment modules already retained.

title: Modulation (NEETS Module 12)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on modulation principles: AM/FM/PM theory and waveforms, transmitter block diagrams, keying methods (on-off, frequency-shift, phase-shift), pulse modulation (PAM/PFM/PCM), and demodulation/detector circuits. Source for the carrier/modulation diagrams now on the Radio page's Modulation Types section.

title: Introduction to Test Equipment (NEETS Module 16)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on multimeters and other test equipment: analog (D'Arsonval movement) and digital meter theory, how voltmeters/ammeters/ohmmeters actually work internally, proper connection/measurement technique, and oscilloscope basics. Source for the labeled VOM diagram now on the Field Tools Units page's Multimeter & Measurement Basics section.

title: Calculus Made Easy (Thompson, 1910)
snippet: A famously accessible introduction to differential and integral calculus - the ideas of rates of change and accumulation explained plainly, without the dense formalism of a typical modern textbook. Retained as a historical public-domain work for a durable, non-safety-critical subject (calculus, like geometry, hasn't changed since publication).

title: NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards
snippet: Quick-reference safety information for hundreds of individual chemicals: exposure limits, physical/chemical properties, health effects, personal protective equipment, and first-aid measures. A safe general reference for identifying and understanding chemical hazards - not a set of hazardous procedures. Opens a new Materials & Chemical Safety Reference category.

title: Linux Fundamentals
snippet: A practical, hands-on Linux system administration course: the shell, filesystem hierarchy, permissions, users/groups, processes, package management, and text processing. Aimed at novice Linux sysadmins - directly relevant to understanding and maintaining this PirateBox's own underlying Raspberry Pi OS. Fills the previously-empty Raspberry Pi / Linux / Networking category alongside the companion Linux Networking book below.

title: Linux Networking
snippet: A practical Linux networking course: TCP/IP and IPv4 fundamentals, DNS, DHCP, SSH client/server, iptables firewalls, and Samba file sharing. Directly addresses the Computing/Networking depth gap (TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP) with a dedicated, hands-on-oriented book rather than a general overview.

title: Tools and Their Uses (NAVEDTRA 14256)
snippet: Navy self-study training course on hand tools and precision measuring tools: types and proper uses of a large range of tools, safety practices, general care, and reading measuring scales/calipers/micrometers. Directly complements the Fastener Design Manual and Basic Machines with the hand-tool and measurement side of Mechanical & Basic Repair - a candidate deferred twice in earlier rounds on access grounds, successfully located this round.

title: A First Course in Physics (Millikan & Gale, 1906)
snippet: A comprehensive introductory physics textbook covering mechanics, heat, sound, light, magnetism, and electricity from first principles, with worked examples throughout. Co-authored by Robert Millikan, later a Nobel laureate in Physics. Retained as a historical public-domain work - the physical principles covered (Newton's laws, energy conservation, basic circuits, optics) remain valid; only the era-specific apparatus/units occasionally show their age.

title: Introduction to Circuit Protection, Control, and Measurement (NEETS Module 3)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on fuses/circuit breakers, switches/relays, and electrical measuring instruments beyond the basic multimeter (meter movements, ammeter/voltmeter/ohmmeter shunts and multipliers, wattmeters, and the safety practices around using them). Rounds out the DC-fundamentals (Module 1) and test-equipment (Module 16) coverage with the protection/control layer between them.

title: Introduction to Solid-State Devices and Power Supplies (NEETS Module 7)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on semiconductor fundamentals: diodes, transistors (bipolar and field-effect), rectifier circuits, and power supply filtering/regulation. The solid-state complement to Module 1's DC fundamentals - covers the components that make up virtually all modern electronics, from the ground up.

title: Microwave Principles (NEETS Module 11)
snippet: Navy self-study training module on microwave-frequency RF theory: waveguides, microwave oscillators (klystrons, magnetrons), and microwave amplifiers (TWTs). Extends the wave-propagation/antenna (Module 10) and modulation (Module 12) coverage into the microwave/UHF-and-above regime, where transmission-line theory gives way to waveguide theory.

title: National Risk Register (UK, 2025 edition)
snippet: The UK government's own comprehensive assessment of the most serious risks it plans against: natural hazards (flooding, wildfire, earthquake, severe space weather, storms, heatwaves, drought, pandemic), infrastructure/technological failures, and security threats, each with a risk summary and preparedness guidance. Complements the existing US-centric emergency content and the already-retained UK Cabinet Office community guide with a broader, current UK government hazard framework - this library's third non-US document.

title: Hazard Communication Standard Pictogram QuickCard (OSHA 3491)
snippet: The nine GHS hazard pictograms used on chemical labels worldwide under the Hazard Communication Standard - health hazard, flame, exclamation mark, gas cylinder, corrosion, exploding bomb, flame over circle, environment, and skull and crossbones - with what each one means. A short, authoritative label-reading reference.

title: Hazard Communication Safety Data Sheets QuickCard (OSHA 3514)
snippet: How a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is organized under the Hazard Communication Standard's required 16-section format - identification, hazards, composition, first-aid, handling/storage, exposure controls/PPE, and more - so an SDS can actually be read and used, not just filed away.

title: Fact Sheet on Compatible Chemical Storage (NIH)
snippet: A concise lettered Chemical Storage Group scheme (compatible organic/inorganic acids and bases, oxidizers, pyrophorics, etc.) for keeping incompatible chemicals safely separated, plus secondary-containment sizing guidance. Fills a real gap the round-7/8 Materials & Chemical Safety page could only describe in general terms without a dedicated compatibility-grouping source.

title: Chemical Segregation and Storage (NIH)
snippet: A practical overview of the three fundamentals of safe chemical storage - maintaining an inventory, identifying hazards via labels/SDS, and understanding compatibility - plus a storage-area inspection checklist (container integrity, signs of chemical degradation, improper storage). Complements the shorter Compatible Chemical Storage fact sheet above with the reasoning behind it.

title: Document Library
snippet: Catalog of manuals and reference documents stored on this device.

title: Field Tools
snippet: Time/date, unit conversion, and coordinate calculators for offline field use.

title: Time & Date
snippet: Current local/UTC time, ISO-8601, Unix timestamp, elapsed-time calculator, day of year.

title: Temperature Converter
snippet: Celsius to Fahrenheit and back.

title: Distance / Mass / Volume / Speed / Pressure Converter
snippet: mm/cm/m/km/in/ft/yd/mi, g/kg/oz/lb, mL/L/US fl oz/cups/pints/quarts/gallons, mph/km/h/m/s, PSI/kPa/bar.

title: Storage / Percentage Converter
snippet: Bytes/KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB, percentage-of and percent-change calculators.

title: Electrical & Battery Runtime
snippet: Volts x Amps = Watts, amp-hours to watt-hours, and a theoretical battery runtime estimate.

title: Electrical Quick Reference
snippet: Ohm's Law and power relationships, common copper wire gauge (AWG) ampacity reference.

title: Multimeter & Measurement Basics
snippet: Continuity, DC voltage, resistance, and current measurement basics, with a labeled VOM diagram - not a live/mains-circuit procedure.

title: Coordinate Converter
snippet: Decimal degrees to/from degrees-minutes-seconds (DMS).

title: Morse Code Converter
snippet: Text to/from International Morse Code, entirely offline, works without JavaScript.

title: Subnet Calculator
snippet: IPv4 network/broadcast address, usable host range, and prefix to/from netmask.

title: Frequency / Wavelength Calculator
snippet: Free-space wavelength from a frequency, plus half-wave and quarter-wave antenna reference lengths.

title: Ohm's Law Solver
snippet: Enter any two of voltage, current, resistance, or power to solve for the other two.

title: Checksum / Hash Calculator
snippet: Verify a file already on this PirateBox, or hash pasted text (SHA-256/MD5).

title: About This PirateBox
snippet: What this device is, what's installed, and its current health - the same public-safe status the Stats page already shows, organized around self-description.
